questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

This question evaluates practical performance engineering skills for NIC interrupt handling in multi-tenant data ingestion workloads. It requires understanding the interplay between kernel networking, IRQ affinity, multiqueue configuration, and per-tenant CPU pinning.

## Key Concepts

- **IRQ Affinity & CPU Isolation**: Direct NIC interrupts to dedicated cores to avoid contention with tenant workloads.
- **NIC Multiqueue, RPS/XPS, & XDP**: Utilize multiple hardware queues and software steering to distribute packet processing.
- **cpuset/cgroups v2**: Enforce per-tenant CPU placement and resource boundaries.
- **Observability**: Use perf, ftrace, bpftrace, and latency histograms for granular visibility.
- **Safe Testing**: Implement staged load testing with automated rollback procedures.

## Code Example

```bash
# Enable IRQ affinity for NIC (eth0) IRQs
for irq in $(cat /proc/interrupts | grep eth0 | awk '{print $1}' | tr -d ':'); do
    echo 2 > /proc/irq/$irq/smp_affinity  # Pin to CPU core 1
done

# Configure RPS for RX distribution across cores 4-7
echo f0 > /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/rx-0/rps_cpus
echo f0 > /sys/class/net/eth0/queues/rx-1/rps_cpus

# Disable irqbalance
systemctl stop irqbalance

# cgroups v2 per-tenant CPU pinning
mkdir -p /sys/fs/cgroup/tenant-a
echo 4-7 > /sys/fs/cgroup/tenant-a/cpuset.cpus.effective
echo 0 > /sys/fs/cgroup/tenant-a/cpuset.mems
echo $(pgrep -f tenant-a-ingestion) > /sys/fs/cgroup/tenant-a/cgroup.procs
```

## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical, beginner-friendly systemd/cgroup isolation for CI workers.

## Key Concepts
- systemd slices and resource controls (CPUQuota, MemoryLimit, TasksMax)
- cgroup v2 awareness and per-job isolation
- test harness for bursts and verification

## Code Example
```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/ci.slice
[Unit]
Description=CI Job Sandbox

[Slice]
CPUAccounting=true
CPUQuota=50%
CPUQuotaPeriodSec=100ms
MemoryLimit=2G
TasksMax=200
```
```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/ci-job@.service
[Unit]
Description=CI Job %I

[Service]
Slice=ci.slice
ExecStart=/bin/sleep infinity
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you extend this for GPU-accelerated jobs?
- How to monitor and automatically eject misbehaving jobs between bursts?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests knowledge of systemd timers, isolation, monitoring, and rollback in production.

## Key Concepts
- systemd timers: OnCalendar, Persistent, AccuracySec, RandomizedDelaySec
- Service isolation: CPUQuota, LimitNOFILE, PrivateTmp, ProtectSystem
- Observability: journald alerts, watchdog
- Rollback plan

## Code Example
```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/batch.timer
[Timer]
OnCalendar=hourly
Persistent=true
AccuracySec=1s
RandomizedDelaySec=30s

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```
```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/batch.service
[Service]
User=batch
Group=batch
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/batch-runner
LimitNOFILE=1048576
CPUQuota=50%
PrivateTmp=true
ProtectSystem=full
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you validate timer drift under simulated load?
- How to implement a safe rollback if drift increases?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question provides a practical, beginner-friendly exercise in network QoS isolation for multi-tenant CI workloads, focusing on real commands and testability rather than pure theory.

## Key Concepts
- Linux tc, HTB (Hierarchical Token Bucket), and fq_codel for fair queuing
- cgroups/net_cls for per-tenant traffic mapping
- iperf3 for throughput and latency baselining
- Rollback procedures and safe default restoration

## Solution
```bash
# Remove any existing qdiscs on eth0
sudo tc qdisc del dev eth0 root 2>/dev/null

# Set up HTB root qdisc with default class (falls back to class 1:40 if no match)
sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root handle 1: htb default 40

# Create 4 tenant classes at 200 Mbps each (total 800 Mbps)
sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1: classid 1:10 htb rate 200mbit ceil 200mbit
sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1: classid 1:20 htb rate 200mbit ceil 200mbit
sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1: classid 1:30 htb rate 200mbit ceil 200mbit
sudo tc class add dev eth0 parent 1: classid 1:40 htb rate 200mbit ceil 200mbit

# Attach fq_codel to each class for low-latency scheduling
for class in 10 20 30 40; do
    sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 parent 1:$class fq_codel
done

# Tag tenant processes using cgroups v1 net_cls
# Create cgroups and set classid (format: major:minor = 1:classid in hex)
mkdir -p /sys/fs/cgroup/tenantA
echo 0x0010001a > /sys/fs/cgroup/tenantA/net_cls.classid  # 1:10 in hex

mkdir -p /sys/fs/cgroup/tenantB
echo 0x00100028 > /sys/fs/cgroup/tenantB/net_cls.classid  # 1:20 in hex

mkdir -p /sys/fs/cgroup/tenantC
echo 0x00100032 > /sys/fs/cgroup/tenantC/net_cls.classid  # 1:30 in hex

mkdir -p /sys/fs/cgroup/tenantD
echo 0x0010003c > /sys/fs/cgroup/tenantD/net_cls.classid  # 1:40 in hex

# Add tc filter to match cgroup traffic
sudo tc filter add dev eth0 parent 1: handle 0x1 cgroup
```

## Test Plan
1. **Baseline**: Run iperf3 server on the host and clients from tenant VMs/containers to measure raw throughput and latency without QoS
2. **Apply QoS**: Apply the tc rules above
3. **Validate**: Each tenant should get ~200 Mbps when all are active; verify latency remains low via ping or tcprtt; confirm isolation by saturating one tenant and checking others are not starved
4. **Monitor**: Use `tc -s class show dev eth0` to view class statistics

## Rollback
```bash
# Remove all tc rules instantly
sudo tc qdisc del dev eth0 root

# Verify default (unlimited) behavior is restored
sudo tc qdisc show dev eth0
```
